claims.claim: Mutation of Arg-6 in human Isd11 ablates binding to ACP.
claims.source: Yeast and human Isd11 retain a conserved Arg-6 residues upstream of the LYR motif (Figure 2A) that electrostatically stabilizes the negatively charged oxygen atoms of the Ppant group in the ACP-Isd11 complex (Cory et al., 2017; Boniecki et al., 2017; Herrera et al., 2019), and mutation of this Arg ablates binding of human Isd11 to ACP (Majmudar et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claims.claim: P. falciparum Isd11 has replaced Arg-6 with an Ile residue.
claims.source: The parasite Isd11, however, has replaced Arg-6 with an Ile residue (Figure 2A) expected to more favorably interact with the local hydrophobic surface of mACP created by Ser-to-Phe substitution.
claims.evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Parasite Isd11 has co-evolved with mACP to optimize formation of the mACP-Isd11 complex in P. falciparum in the absence of FASII and an acyl-Ppant group on mACP.
claims.source: These sequence features suggest that parasite Isd11 has co-evolved with mACP to optimize formation of the mACP-Isd11 complex in P. falciparum in the absence of FASII and an acyl-Ppant group on mACP.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the sequence changes in both mACP (Ser to Phe) and Isd11 (Arg to Ile) that are complementary.

claims.claim: Recombinant parasite Isd11 expressed in bacteria did not co-purify with the endogenous ~9 kDa E. coli ACP.
claims.source: Consistent with this model, recombinantly parasite Isd11 expressed in bacteria did not co-purify with the endogenous ~9 kDa E. coli ACP (Figure 2G) or with coexpressed apicoplast ACP (Figure 2—figure supplement 7), both of which retain the conserved Ser and Ppant modification.
claims.evidence: This is supported by SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: Recombinant parasite Isd11 expressed in bacteria did not co-purify with coexpressed apicoplast ACP.
claims.source: Consistent with this model, recombinantly parasite Isd11 expressed in bacteria did not co-purify with the endogenous ~9 kDa E. coli ACP (Figure 2G) or with coexpressed apicoplast ACP (Figure 2—figure supplement 7), both of which retain the conserved Ser and Ppant modification.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claims.claim: Human Isd11 robustly binds bacterial ACP when expressed in E. coli.
claims.source: This specificity by P. falciparum Isd11 contrasts with that of human Isd11, which robustly binds bacterial ACP when expressed in E. coli (Cory et al., 2017; Boniecki et al., 2017; Cai et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claims.claim: Association of Isd11 and mACP in yeast and human cells depends critically on the acyl-Ppant group of mACP.
claims.source: Association of Isd11 and mACP in yeast and human cells depends critically on the acyl-Ppant group of mACP (Figure 3A), with little or no association observed in these cells between Isd11 and the mACP Ser-to-Ala mutant that lacks a Ppant group (Van Vranken et al., 2016; Van Vranken et al., 2018; Majmudar et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claims.claim: Little or no association is observed in yeast and human cells between Isd11 and the mACP Ser-to-Ala mutant that lacks a Ppant group.
claims.source: Association of Isd11 and mACP in yeast and human cells depends critically on the acyl-Ppant group of mACP (Figure 3A), with little or no association observed in these cells between Isd11 and the mACP Ser-to-Ala mutant that lacks a Ppant group (Van Vranken et al., 2016; Van Vranken et al., 2018; Majmudar et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claims.claim: The mACP-Isd11 interface in yeast and humans includes key electrostatic interactions between conserved Lys and Arg residues in Isd11 and Glu and Asp residues in mACP.
claims.source: The mACP-Isd11 interface in these organisms also includes key electrostatic interactions between conserved Lys and Arg residues in Isd11 and Glu and Asp residues in mACP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Cory et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior structural studies and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The Rosetta structural model suggests that the unusual Phe113 residue of mACP partitions into a hydrophobic pocket at the mACP-Isd11 interface.
claims.source: The resulting low-energy structural model suggested that the unusual Phe113 residue of mACP partitions into a hydrophobic pocket at the mACP-Isd11 interface composed of the aliphatic side-chain methylene groups of Lys10 and Arg14 and the phenyl ring of Tyr13 of Isd11 as well as Val117 on mACP (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is based on computational structural modeling shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The predicted mACP-Isd11 binding interface includes conserved electrostatic interactions between basic residues on parasite Isd11 and acidic groups on mACP.
claims.source: The predicted binding interface also included conserved electrostatic interactions between basic residues on parasite Isd11 and acidic groups on mACP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on computational structural modeling shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: WT mACP-HA2 but not the F113A mutant co-purified with Isd11 in Ni-NTA pulldown experiments from E. coli.
claims.source: We then used Ni-NTA to selectively pull down His-tagged Isd11 and observed that WT mACP-HA2 but not the F113A mutant co-purified with Isd11 (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Mutation of Phe113 to Ala substantially weakens the mACP-Isd11 interaction.
claims.source: These results indicate that mutation of Phe113 to Ala substantially weakens the mACP-Isd11 interaction, supporting the conclusion that Phe113 contributes to the mACP-Isd11 binding interface in the mACP-Isd11-Nfs1 complex as suggested by structural modeling (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the loss of co-purification in the F113A mutant shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Parasites expressing a second copy of WT mACP showed identical growth in the presence or absence of aTc.
claims.source: Parasites expressing a second copy of WT mACP showed identical growth in the presence or absence of aTc. In contrast, parasites that episomally expressed the F113A mACP mutant showed strongly diminished growth upon aTc removal and loss of endogenous mACP (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Parasites that episomally expressed the F113A mACP mutant showed strongly diminished growth upon aTc removal and loss of endogenous mACP.
claims.source: Parasites expressing a second copy of WT mACP showed identical growth in the presence or absence of aTc. In contrast, parasites that episomally expressed the F113A mACP mutant showed strongly diminished growth upon aTc removal and loss of endogenous mACP (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: The Phe residue of mACP plays a key role in stabilizing the mACP-Isd11 association required for Nfs1 stability and function.
claims.source: These results support the conclusion that the Phe residue of mACP plays a key role in stabilizing the mACP-Isd11 association required for Nfs1 stability and function.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the inability of the F113A mutant to rescue parasite growth upon endogenous mACP knockdown (Figure 3D).

claims.claim: Nfs1 stability in other eukaryotes depends critically on its association with Isd11 and ACP.
claims.source: Nfs1 stability in other eukaryotes depends critically on its association with Isd11 and ACP, with loss of ACP resulting in degradation of Nfs1 and lethal defects in Fe-S cluster biogenesis (Van Vranken et al., 2016; Cory et al., 2017; Boniecki et al., 2017; Lill and Freibert, 2020; Cai et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claims.claim: Loss of ACP in other eukaryotes results in degradation of Nfs1 and lethal defects in Fe-S cluster biogenesis.
claims.source: Nfs1 stability in other eukaryotes depends critically on its association with Isd11 and ACP, with loss of ACP resulting in degradation of Nfs1 and lethal defects in Fe-S cluster biogenesis (Van Vranken et al., 2016; Cory et al., 2017; Boniecki et al., 2017; Lill and Freibert, 2020; Cai et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claims.claim: The commercial anti-Nfs1 antibody (Abcam 229829) selectively recognized recombinant P. falciparum Nfs1 expressed in E. coli.
claims.source: To test the impact of mACP knockdown on Nfs1 protein levels in parasites, we used a commercial anti-Nfs1 antibody (Abcam 229829) raised against a 250-amino acid region of human Nfs1 that is 55% identical to P. falciparum Nfs1 and that selectively recognized recombinant P. falciparum Nfs1 expressed in E. coli (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In parasites grown +aTc, the anti-Nfs1 antibody recognized a band at ~60 kDa.
claims.source: In parasites grown +aTc, the anti-Nfs1 antibody recognized a band at ~60 kDa (Figure 4A) that is close to the predicted molecular mass of 63 kDa for this protein.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: WB analysis of parasites grown in -aTc conditions failed to detect the ~60 kDa Nfs1 band.
claims.source: WB analysis of parasites grown in -aTc conditions failed to detect this ~60 kDa band (Figure 4A), strongly suggesting that Nfs1 stability is tightly coupled to mACP expression and that loss of mACP results in Nfs1 degradation in parasites as it does in yeast (Van Vranken et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Nfs1 stability is tightly coupled to mACP expression in P. falciparum.
claims.source: WB analysis of parasites grown in -aTc conditions failed to detect this ~60 kDa band (Figure 4A), strongly suggesting that Nfs1 stability is tightly coupled to mACP expression and that loss of mACP results in Nfs1 degradation in parasites as it does in yeast (Van Vranken et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the loss of Nfs1 signal upon mACP knockdown shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Loss of mACP results in Nfs1 degradation in P. falciparum parasites.
claims.source: WB analysis of parasites grown in -aTc conditions failed to detect this ~60 kDa band (Figure 4A), strongly suggesting that Nfs1 stability is tightly coupled to mACP expression and that loss of mACP results in Nfs1 degradation in parasites as it does in yeast (Van Vranken et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the loss of Nfs1 signal upon mACP knockdown shown in Figure 4A and is consistent with prior work in yeast.

claims.claim: The epitope-tagged Rieske band was detected ~43 kDa in WB analysis of parasites grown + aTc.
claims.source: A band corresponding to the epitope-tagged Rieske was detected ~43 kDa in WB analysis of parasites grown + aTc. This band, however, was undetectable in parasites grown 72 hr in -aTc conditions to downregulate mACP expression (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The Rieske band was undetectable in parasites grown 72 hr in -aTc conditions to downregulate mACP expression.
claims.source: A band corresponding to the epitope-tagged Rieske was detected ~43 kDa in WB analysis of parasites grown + aTc. This band, however, was undetectable in parasites grown 72 hr in -aTc conditions to downregulate mACP expression (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Knockdown of mACP and subsequent degradation of Nfs1 are accompanied by loss of the Fe-S cluster-dependent Rieske protein.
claims.source: These results indicate that knockdown of mACP and subsequent degradation of Nfs1 are accompanied by loss of the Fe-S cluster-dependent Rieske protein.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the Western blot data showing loss of both Nfs1 and Rieske upon mACP knockdown (Figure 4A, 4B).

claims.claim: Loss of mACP in -aTc conditions did not reduce expression levels of the mitochondrial chaperone HSP60.
claims.source: The impact of mACP knockdown on stability of Nfs1 and Rieske was specific to these proteins as loss of mACP in -aTc conditions did not reduce expression levels of the mitochondrial chaperone HSP60 or the integral ETC complex III component, cyt c1 (Figure 4B and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Loss of mACP in -aTc conditions did not reduce expression levels of the integral ETC complex III component, cyt c1.
claims.source: The impact of mACP knockdown on stability of Nfs1 and Rieske was specific to these proteins as loss of mACP in -aTc conditions did not reduce expression levels of the mitochondrial chaperone HSP60 or the integral ETC complex III component, cyt c1 (Figure 4B and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The Rieske protein is an essential electron-transfer component of ETC complex III.
claims.source: Since the Rieske protein is an essential electron-transfer component of ETC complex III (Zhang et al., 1998), we reasoned that loss of mACP and Rieske likely results in ETC failure.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claims.claim: In blood-stage parasites, the essential function of the mitochondrial ETC is to oxidatively recycle the ubiquinone cofactor used by several dehydrogenases, of which dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHOD) is most critical.
claims.source: In blood-stage parasites, which rely on glycolysis rather than oxidative phosphorylation for ATP synthesis, the essential function of the mitochondrial ETC is to oxidatively recycle the ubiquinone cofactor used by several dehydrogenases, of which dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHOD) is most critical (Painter et al., 2007; Ke et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claims.claim: Exogenous addition of decyl-ubiquinone (dQ) rescues parasites from ETC dysfunction caused by the ETC complex III inhibitor, atovaquone.
claims.source: Prior work has shown that exogenous addition of the soluble ubiquinone analog, decyl-ubiquinone (dQ), rescues parasites from ETC dysfunction caused by the ETC complex III inhibitor, atovaquone (Ke et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claims.claim: 15 µM exogenous dQ substantially rescued parasites over multiple intraerythrocytic cycles from growth inhibition by 100 nM atovaquone.
claims.source: As a positive control and to provide a basis for comparison, we first confirmed that 15 µM exogenous dQ substantially rescued parasites over multiple intraerythrocytic cycles from growth inhibition by 100 nM atovaquone (Figure 5A), as previously reported (Ke et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Parasites cultured -aTc grew normally for 3 days but failed to expand into the third growth cycle on day 4.
claims.source: As before, -aTc parasites grew normally for 3 days but failed to expand into the third growth cycle on day 4 (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Addition of dQ rescued parasite growth in the third growth cycle in -aTc conditions.
claims.source: Addition of dQ rescued parasite growth in the third growth cycle in -aTc conditions, similar to dQ rescue of parasites from atovaquone.
claims.evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: dQ only rescued the third-cycle growth of parasites cultured -aTc, which failed to expand further and began to die off on day 6 in the fourth intraerythrocytic cycle.
claims.source: However, in contrast to indefinite parasite rescue from atovaquone, dQ only rescued the third-cycle growth of parasites cultured -aTc, which failed to expand further and began to die off on day 6 in the fourth intraerythrocytic cycle (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: ETC failure is the immediate cause of parasite death upon mACP knockdown.
claims.source: On the basis of dQ rescue, we conclude that ETC failure is the immediate cause of parasite death upon mACP knockdown.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the ability of dQ to rescue parasites in the third cycle shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Additional dysfunctions beyond the mitochondrial ETC contribute to parasite death on a longer timescale upon mACP knockdown.
claims.source: However, the inability of dQ to rescue parasites beyond the third cycle indicates that additional dysfunctions beyond the mitochondrial ETC contribute to parasite death on a longer timescale.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the failure of dQ to rescue parasites beyond the third cycle shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The ETC couples ubiquinone recycling to proton translocation from the mitochondrial matrix to the inner membrane space to establish a transmembrane electrochemical potential.
claims.source: The ETC couples ubiquinone recycling to proton translocation from the mitochondrial matrix to the inner membrane space to establish a transmembrane electrochemical potential.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about ETC function.

claims.claim: Parasites retain a second proton-pumping mechanism that also contributes to transmembrane potential and that is inhibited by proguanil.
claims.source: Prior work has shown that parasites retain a second proton-pumping mechanism that also contributes to transmembrane potential and that is inhibited by proguanil (Painter et al., 2007; Skinner-Adams et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claims.claim: Inhibition of ETC function kills parasites due to defective ubiquinone recycling but does not substantially depolarize mitochondria due to activity by the proguanil-sensitive pathway.
claims.source: Inhibition of ETC function kills parasites due to defective ubiquinone recycling but does not substantially depolarize mitochondria due to activity by this second, proguanil-sensitive pathway.
claims.evidence: This is based on prior published work cited in the manuscript.

claims.claim: ETC dysfunction plus proguanil treatment blocks both pathways for proton pumping and causes mitochondrial depolarization.
claims.source: However, ETC dysfunction plus proguanil treatment blocks both pathways for proton pumping and causes mitochondrial depolarization, which can be visualized by a failure to concentrate charged dyes like MitoTracker within the mitochondrion that leads to dispersed dye accumulation in the cytoplasm (Painter et al., 2007; Ke et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claims.claim: Parasite treatment with sublethal proguanil negated the ability of dQ to rescue parasite growth from mACP knockdown in the third cycle.
claims.source: We repeated the prior growth assay ± aTc and ±dQ but also included 1 µM proguanil. This proguanil concentration alone had no effect on parasite growth, as previously reported (Painter et al., 2007). However, when proguanil was combined with growth -aTc, dQ was unable to rescue parasite growth in the third cycle (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Proguanil treatment selectively prevented mitochondrial accumulation of MitoTracker Red in parasites grown -aTc.
claims.source: Microscopy analysis of parasites on day 3 of the growth assay revealed that proguanil treatment selectively prevented mitochondrial accumulation of MitoTracker Red in parasites grown -aTc, strongly suggesting mitochondrial depolarization (Figure 5C and D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5C, 5D, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Impaired ubiquinone recycling due to Rieske loss and ETC dysfunction is the immediate cause of parasite death upon mACP knockdown.
claims.source: This observation strongly supports the model that impaired ubiquinone recycling due to Rieske loss and ETC dysfunction is the immediate cause of parasite death upon mACP knockdown.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the dQ rescue and mitochondrial depolarization experiments shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The P. falciparum mitochondrion is a major antimalarial drug target.
claims.source: The P. falciparum mitochondrion is a major antimalarial drug target, but nearly all organelle-specific inhibitors target cytochrome b in ETC complex III or DHOD that depends on complex III function (Antonova-Koch et al., 2018; Goodman et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claims.claim: Nearly all organelle-specific inhibitors target cytochrome b in ETC complex III or DHOD that depends on complex III function.
claims.source: The P. falciparum mitochondrion is a major antimalarial drug target, but nearly all organelle-specific inhibitors target cytochrome b in ETC complex III or DHOD that depends on complex III function (Antonova-Koch et al., 2018; Goodman et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claims.claim: Many mitochondrial metabolic pathways are dispensable for blood-stage parasites.
claims.source: Multiple metabolic pathways operate within the mitochondrion (van Dooren et al., 2006), but many are dispensable for blood-stage parasites, and few essential blood-stage functions beyond DHOD and ETC complexes III and IV have been identified.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work and represents established knowledge.

claims.claim: ISC biosynthesis is an ancient, essential mitochondrial function that has been well studied in yeast and mammalian cells but is sparsely studied in parasites.
claims.source: ISC biosynthesis is an ancient, essential mitochondrial function that has been well studied in yeast and mammalian cells but is sparsely studied in parasites (Gisselberg et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work and represents established knowledge.

claims.claim: Most eukaryotic cells retain a mitochondrial FASII pathway in which the acyl-ACP intermediate critically mediates respiratory chain assembly, Fe-S cluster biogenesis, and ribosomal translation by binding to LYR-protein assembly factors.
claims.source: Most eukaryotic cells, including fungi, plants, and animals, retain a mitochondrial FASII pathway in which the acyl-ACP intermediate has been shown to critically mediate respiratory chain assembly, Fe-S cluster biogenesis, and ribosomal translation by binding to LYR-protein assembly factors (Majmudar et al., 2019; Angerer, 2015; Nowinski et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claims.claim: ACP interactions with LYR proteins and their dependence on ACP acylation have been proposed to constitute a regulatory feedback mechanism that couples the availability of acetyl-CoA for FASII activity to respiratory chain assembly for oxidative phosphorylation and ATP synthesis.
claims.source: These interactions and their dependence on ACP acylation have been proposed to constitute a regulatory feedback mechanism that couples the availability of acetyl-CoA for FASII activity to respiratory chain assembly for oxidative phosphorylation and ATP synthesis (Van Vranken et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claims.claim: Biochemical coupling of FASII and respiratory chain assembly has not been retained in Plasmodium.
claims.source: Biochemical coupling of these pathways, however, has not been retained in Plasmodium, which has lost mitochondrial FASII enzymes but retains a divergent ACP homolog incapable of 4-Ppant modification or acylation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the loss of mitochondrial FASII enzymes and the Ser-to-Phe substitution in mACP.

claims.claim: mACP remains essential to parasites for Fe-S cluster biogenesis by binding to Isd11.
claims.source: Nevertheless, we have shown that mACP remains essential to parasites for Fe-S cluster biogenesis by binding to Isd11, which is the only LYR-protein homolog retained by P. falciparum.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the growth assay data (Figure 1E), co-IP experiments (Figure 2D, 2F, 2G), and loss of Nfs1 upon mACP knockdown (Figure 4A).

claims.claim: Isd11 binds to mACP via a novel molecular interface.
claims.source: Isd11 binds to mACP via a novel interface molecular interface, and this interaction is critical stabilizing the mACP-Isd11-Nfs1 cysteine desulfurase complex.
claims.evidence: This is supported by structural modeling (Figure 3B) and mutagenesis studies (Figure 3C, 3D).

claims.claim: P. falciparum provides a new molecular paradigm for essential ACP function without an acyl-Ppant group.
claims.source: P. falciparum thus provides a new molecular paradigm for essential ACP function without an acyl-Ppant group.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the collective findings showing mACP essentiality and function without a Ppant group.

claims.claim: Prior in vitro work has provided evidence that activity of purified Isd11-Nfs1 does not strictly require association with ACP.
claims.source: Prior in vitro work has provided evidence that activity of purified Isd11-Nfs1 does not strictly require association with ACP (Boniecki et al., 2017; Lill and Freibert, 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claims.claim: Nfs1 is unstable in its native mitochondrial context in the absence of ACP in P. falciparum and yeast.
claims.source: However, Nfs1 is unstable in its native mitochondrial context in the absence of ACP, as shown herein for P. falciparum and in prior studies of yeast (Van Vranken et al., 2016; Adam et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing loss of Nfs1 upon mACP knockdown (Figure 4A) and citations to prior work in yeast.

results.result: P. falciparum has lost mitochondrial FASII enzymes but retains a divergent mitochondrial ACP (mACP) that lacks the conserved serine residue required for 4-phosphopantetheine (Ppant) modification, having replaced it with phenylalanine.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C20, C28, C36, and C37 are well-supported by BLAST analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) showing absence of mitochondrial FASII enzymes and sequence alignment data (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2) demonstrating the Ser-to-Phe substitution in mACP. The consistency between sequence analysis, prior citations, and phylogenetic data provides strong evidence for this structural divergence.

results.result: P. falciparum mACP localizes to the mitochondrion and undergoes post-translational processing upon import, with the mature protein beginning at or near Leu-51.
results.evaluation: Claims C32, C38, C39, C40, C41, C42, and C43 are supported by immunofluorescence colocalization with HSP60 (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 3), Western blot analysis showing size differences between predicted (21 kDa) and observed (15 kDa) molecular mass (Figure 1C), and mass spectrometry data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2). The co-migration of truncated Δ2-50 mACP with parasite-expressed mACP provides strong evidence for the processing site.

results.result: mACP is essential for P. falciparum blood-stage parasite viability, as demonstrated by ligand-dependent knockdown experiments showing parasite death in the third intraerythrocytic cycle upon mACP depletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C6, C33, C44, C45, C46, and C47 are strongly supported by growth assay data (Figure 1E) showing normal growth for 3 days followed by major growth defect on day 4 in -aTc conditions, blood-smear analysis showing widespread parasite death (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), and Western blot confirmation of robust mACP knockdown (Figure 1E inset). The temporal pattern and reproducibility support essentiality.

results.result: P. falciparum lacks homologs of most LYR-motif proteins found in other eukaryotes but retains Isd11 (PF3D7_1311000), which shares 29% identity with human Isd11 and conserves the LYR sequence motif.
results.evaluation: Claims C52, C53, C54, C55, and C56 are supported by comprehensive BLAST analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) with appropriate e-value cutoffs (3e-6 for Isd11, >0.01 for others) and sequence alignment data (Figure 2A) showing conservation of the LYR motif. The systematic search methodology and clear e-value thresholds provide confidence in the negative results for other LYR proteins.

results.result: P. falciparum mACP directly binds to Isd11 via the LYR motif and stabilizes the Isd11-Nfs1 complex required for Fe-S cluster biosynthesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C34, C62, C64, C65, C68, C69, C70, and C71 are strongly supported by multiple lines of evidence: mass spectrometry showing Nfs1 enrichment in mACP-HA2 IP samples (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), reciprocal co-IP experiments in parasites (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 4) and E. coli (Figure 2F), LYR mutagenesis studies showing reduced/eliminated binding (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 4), and purification of 1:1 mACP-Isd11 complex (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 6). The convergence of multiple experimental approaches provides robust support.

results.result: P. falciparum mACP binds Isd11 through a divergent molecular interface that does not require the Ppant group, with parasite Isd11 having replaced the conserved Arg-6 with isoleucine to accommodate the hydrophobic Phe113 of mACP.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C35, C74, C75, C76, and C77 are supported by sequence analysis showing the Arg-to-Ile substitution in parasite Isd11 (Figure 2A), co-IP experiments demonstrating mACP-Isd11 interaction despite lack of Ppant (Figure 2D, 2F, 2G), and specificity experiments showing parasite Isd11 does not bind E. coli ACP or apicoplast ACP (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 7). The complementary sequence changes and binding specificity support co-evolution.

results.result: Structural modeling and mutagenesis studies demonstrate that Phe113 of mACP partitions into a hydrophobic pocket at the mACP-Isd11 interface and is critical for complex stability and parasite viability.
results.evaluation: Claims C82, C83, C84, C85, C86, C87, and C88 are supported by Rosetta structural modeling (Figure 3B), Ni-NTA pulldown experiments showing loss of co-purification with F113A mutant (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2), and growth assays demonstrating that F113A mACP cannot rescue parasites upon endogenous mACP knockdown (Figure 3D). The integration of computational and experimental validation provides strong support, though the structural model remains a prediction.

results.result: Knockdown of mACP causes loss of Nfs1 protein in P. falciparum parasites, indicating that Nfs1 stability is tightly coupled to mACP expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C91, C92, C93, C94, and C95 are supported by Western blot analysis using a validated anti-Nfs1 antibody (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) showing detection of ~60 kDa Nfs1 band in +aTc conditions but not in -aTc conditions (Figure 4A). The antibody validation in E. coli and appropriate molecular weight provide confidence, though densitometry analysis shows high variability (p=0.2) across replicates (Figure 4D).

results.result: Knockdown of mACP causes loss of the Rieske Fe-S protein in ETC complex III, while other mitochondrial proteins (HSP60, cyt c1) remain stable.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C96, C97, and C98 are supported by Western blot analysis showing loss of epitope-tagged Rieske (~43 kDa) in -aTc conditions (Figure 4B) while HSP60 and cyt c1 levels are maintained (Figure 4B, 4C). The specificity of the effect strengthens the conclusion, though statistical analysis shows marginal significance for Rieske (p=0.07) (Figure 4D).

results.result: Decyl-ubiquinone (dQ) temporarily rescues parasites from death upon mACP knockdown for one intraerythrocytic cycle, indicating that ETC failure is the immediate cause of death but additional dysfunctions contribute to death on longer timescales.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C8, C104, C105, C106, C107, C108, and C109 are supported by growth assay data (Figure 5A) showing dQ rescue in the third cycle but not beyond, compared to indefinite rescue from atovaquone. The temporal pattern of rescue provides strong evidence for ETC dysfunction as the immediate cause of death, with the limitation of rescue indicating additional essential functions. The comparison with atovaquone as a positive control strengthens the interpretation.

results.result: Proguanil treatment prevents dQ rescue and causes mitochondrial depolarization in mACP-depleted parasites, supporting the model that impaired ubiquinone recycling due to Rieske loss and ETC dysfunction is the immediate cause of parasite death.
results.evaluation: Claims C115, C116, and C117 are supported by growth assay data showing loss of dQ rescue with proguanil (Figure 5B) and microscopy analysis showing dispersed MitoTracker signal specifically in -aTc+proguanil conditions (Figure 5C, 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The statistical analysis (p=0.003) and mechanistic consistency with prior work on proguanil strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: The decoupling of mitochondrial Fe-S cluster biogenesis from FASII activity through retention of a Ppant-independent mACP is widespread among apicomplexan parasites (Toxoplasma, Babesia) and the chromerid Vitrella brassicaformis.
results.evaluation: Claims C13, C14, C134, C135, C136, and C137 are supported by sequence analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) showing divergent mACP homologs lacking the conserved Ser in multiple apicomplexan species and V. brassicaformis. The phylogenetic distribution and timing relative to loss of plastid photosynthesis provide evolutionary context, though functional validation in other species is lacking.

results.result: Background knowledge claims about eukaryotic mitochondrial FASII pathways, malaria epidemiology, P. falciparum mitochondrial metabolism, and apicoplast FASII.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C15, C16, C17, C18, C19, C21, C22, C23, C24, C25, C26, and C27 represent established knowledge supported by appropriate citations to prior published work. These provide necessary context for the study but are not novel findings.

results.result: Background knowledge claims about LYR proteins, mACP interactions in yeast and humans, and the Isd11-Nfs1 complex in other eukaryotes.
results.evaluation: Claims C29, C30, C31, C48, C49, C50, C51, C58, C59, C60, C61, C72, C73, C78, C79, C80, C81, C89, and C90 represent established knowledge from prior studies supported by appropriate citations. These provide essential comparative context for understanding the divergent features of the parasite system.

results.result: Background knowledge claims about the parasite ETC, ubiquinone recycling, mitochondrial membrane potential, and antimalarial drug targets.
results.evaluation: Claims C101, C102, C103, C111, C112, C113, C114, C118, C119, C120, and C121 represent established knowledge supported by citations to prior work. These provide necessary mechanistic context for interpreting the dQ rescue and proguanil experiments.

results.result: P. falciparum provides a new molecular paradigm for essential ACP function without an acyl-Ppant group, representing a parasite-specific adaptation that decouples Fe-S cluster biogenesis from FASII activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C122, C123, C124, C125, C126, C127, C128, C129, C130, C131, and C138 synthesize the major findings into a conceptual framework. The conclusion is well-supported by the collective experimental evidence (essentiality, Isd11 binding, Nfs1 stabilization, lack of Ppant) and comparison with other eukaryotes. The paradigm shift is justified by the data.

results.result: Loss of mACP destabilizes Nfs1, impairs Rieske stability and ETC complex III function, and leads to parasite death. P. falciparum lacks MZM1 homolog but retains cyt c1 upon mACP loss, suggesting accumulation of a late complex III assembly intermediate.
results.evaluation: Claims C139, C140, C141, C142, C143, C144, and C145 integrate multiple experimental observations (Western blots in Figure 4, growth assays in Figure 1E and Figure 5) with comparative analysis (BLAST for MZM1, comparison with yeast). The retention of cyt c1 levels (Figure 4C) supports the assembly intermediate model by analogy to yeast, though direct demonstration of the intermediate is lacking.

results.result: Respiratory failure is the immediate cause of parasite death upon mACP loss, but defects in other essential processes (potentially involving mitochondrial fumarate hydratase and/or cytoplasmic/nuclear Fe-S cluster proteins) contribute to death on longer timescales.
results.evaluation: Claims C146, C147, C148, and C149 are supported by the temporal pattern of dQ rescue (Figure 5A) showing rescue in cycle 3 but not beyond. However, C149 is speculative regarding the specific processes involved, as no direct evidence is provided for fumarate hydratase or cytoplasmic Fe-S cluster protein dysfunction. The inference is reasonable but requires further validation.

results.result: Background and speculative claims about cytoplasmic Fe-S cluster biogenesis, including the potential role of Mdr2 transporter and independence from mitochondrial Nfs1 in mammalian cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C150, C151, C152, and C153 are based on prior work in other organisms but lack direct experimental validation in P. falciparum. The dispensability of Mdr2 in blood-stage parasites (C152) and potential independence of cytoplasmic Fe-S cluster synthesis from mitochondrial Nfs1 (C153) create uncertainty about the mechanisms underlying the longer-term lethality of mACP loss.

results.result: P. falciparum mACP does not regulate mitochondrial translation, as evidenced by lack of L0R8F8 homolog, retention of cyt c1 levels upon mACP knockdown, and maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential in -aTc conditions alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C154, C155, C156, C157, C158, C159, C160, and C161 are supported by BLAST analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), Western blot data showing stable cyt c1 (Figure 4C), and microscopy showing focal MitoTracker signal in -aTc conditions (Figure 5C). The convergence of multiple lines of negative evidence (absence of L0R8F8, retention of mitochondrial translation products and membrane potential) provides reasonable support for the conclusion.

results.result: Specificity controls for mACP interactions and effects of mACP knockdown, showing that mACP retains conserved Glu residues for LYR motif interaction, Isd11 was not detected in IP/MS samples, mACP does not interact with HSP60 or cyt c1, and HSP60/cyt c1 levels are maintained upon mACP knockdown.
results.evaluation: Claims C57, C63, C66, C67, C99, and C100 provide important specificity controls. The sequence conservation (C57) is well-documented (Figure 1A). The absence of Isd11 in IP/MS (C63) is explained by its small size. The negative controls for mACP interaction (C66, C67) and protein stability (C99, C100) are supported by co-IP and Western blot data (Figure 2E, Figure 4B, 4C), strengthening the specificity of the mACP-Isd11 interaction and effects on Nfs1/Rieske.

results.result: Speculative claims about additional functional/regulatory roles of ACP in Fe-S cluster biogenesis, comparison with anaerobic parasites lacking ACP/Isd11, and potential for additional mACP interactions in parasites beyond Isd11-Nfs1.
results.evaluation: Claims C132, C133, C162, and C163 are speculative and acknowledge uncertainty. C132 and C162 propose additional functions for mACP beyond those demonstrated, while C133 provides comparative context from other parasites. C163 notes that any additional interactions would diverge from known LYR-protein interactions. These represent reasonable hypotheses for future work but lack direct experimental support.

results.result: Background claim that the mitochondrial ETC is essential for malaria parasite viability in all lifecycle stages.
results.evaluation: Claim C164 is supported by citation to prior published work and represents established knowledge providing context for the therapeutic relevance of the findings.
